problems.form_value: online_rct (the form's agreed_fields_checked says the setting 'is not stated outright', and open_questions repeats the point)
problems.source_says: The paper never says whether the submitters took the Qualtrics session remotely or in a supervised room. They were community college students 'who participated for research credits' (p. 10) through the 'Research Experience Program' (p. 22). That is a student pool, not an online panel, which is the codebook's wording for online_rct. The only hint is the reason given for the control instruction, which cites AI use by 'online survey respondents' in past work. That is an analogy, not a statement of the setting, so online_rct rests on an inference. If the session was supervised, lab_rct applies. Both codes are core, so criterion 1 does not change. The ACM version of record or the OSF preregistration may state the setting.
problems.quote: Given that past work suggests that online survey respondents frequently use AI tools to generate answers (Veselovsky et al., 2023), we explicitly instructed participants in the control condition to not use AI in this task.
problems.locator: p. 11, Method, Submission Phase; p. 10, Participants; p. 22, Acknowledgments; a full-text search for 'online', 'lab', 'remote', 'in person', and 'session' finds no statement of the setting

confirmed.statement: (a) The paper states random assignment: 'After consenting, participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions that varied whether they completed the idea-generation task with or without access to an AI chatbot'. The form's assignment.quote is verbatim. The abstract says participants 'were experimentally assigned to one of three conditions', and Figure A1 draws a shuffle symbol between 'Submitters' and the three arms. The paper does not describe how the randomization was done.
confirmed.locator: p. 11, Method, Submission Phase; p. 2, Abstract; p. 33, Figure A1

confirmed.statement: (a, e) unit = individual and structure = between are right. Each participant was assigned to one of three conditions and did the whole task in it, and Appendix B compares the two AI arms with 'independent-samples t-tests'. The counterbalancing on p. 12 is the order of the three objects, not the order of conditions, so check (e) does not apply.
confirmed.locator: p. 11, Submission Phase; p. 12, Occasions; p. 38, Appendix B, Behavioral Outcomes

confirmed.statement: (b) What was assigned is access to a generative-AI tool for the participant's own ideas. The AI arms 'had access to ChatGPT through an embedded web-app in the Qualtrics survey; they entered their alternative uses below the web-app interface'. The control arm 'had no web-app, just the fields to enter their alternative uses'. Every arm submitted its own ideas, so the conditions do not differ only in whose output is rated. The introduction says the two AI groups 'were told to use AI'.

(c) The tool is a large language model. The AI arms got 'a custom AI chatbot that was designed for the study, which was built on top of gpt-3.5'. Appendix A describes a Vercel web app that 'emulated the generic AI chatbot experience (e.g., ChatGPT)', gpt-3.5 at temperature 0.7, and one helpful-assistant system prompt 'for all interactions with participants'. ai_tool.name_model and role = open_chat match. Page 12 calls the tool 'ChatGPT', and the form follows the more exact description on pp. 11 and 33.
confirmed.locator: p. 11, Submission Phase; p. 33, Appendix A, Web App and Language Model; p. 12, Occasions

confirmed.statement: The arm instructions in the form are verbatim. Figure A1 prints, for High-Agency, 'Instead of asking AI to come up with ideas for you, use it to expand upon your own ideas to generate ones that are even more creative.' and, for Low-Agency, 'Let the AI's creative power work for you. Trust in its ability to generate creative ideas and don't hesitate to use its suggestions directly.' Page 11 has 'The beauty of AI is that it does the heavy lifting for you.' Page 11 calls the Figure A1 texts 'representative excerpts from the instructions'.
confirmed.locator: p. 33, Figure A1; p. 11, Submission Phase

confirmed.statement: (d) The comparison arms match the form. In the control condition 'participants completed the same AUT without access to an AI chatbot', read 'please do NOT use AI during the task', and had copy-paste disabled (that sentence sits in the control passage). So arms[Control].ai = none, and the AI-versus-control contrasts are ai_vs_bau. The two AI arms used the same chatbot and system prompt and differ in the instruction page, which fits ai_design for High-Agency versus Low-Agency. Neither AI arm is uninstructed use, as the form's open_questions say.
confirmed.locator: p. 11, Submission Phase; p. 33, Figure A1 and System Prompt; p. 17, Discussion

confirmed.statement: ai_tool.how_used is supported. 'Each object corresponded to one human-AI interaction', participants typed their uses below the chat window, and the instruction page came before the AUT with a 10-second minimum. The Discussion describes the manipulation as assigning people 'to read one of three common forms of guidance about AI usage', and Future Directions says later studies could make the AI arms 'behave differently, not just think differently'.
confirmed.locator: p. 14, Data Structure; p. 12, Occasions; p. 11, Submission Phase; p. 17, Discussion; p. 21, Future Directions

confirmed.statement: preregistered = yes and prereg_locator are right. 'The study was pre-registered on OSF including hypotheses, power analysis, procedure and analytic approach', and p. 14 lists 'two key deviations from our preregistration': N = 150 instead of 450, and the noncompliance exclusions.

arms[].n_randomized and n_analyzed = null are right. The paper prints no count per arm, only the total N = 150 and the complete exclusions of 12 high-agency and 10 low-agency participants. It does not say whether the three submitters excluded for 'an initial attention check' had been assigned to a condition.
confirmed.locator: p. 10, Participants; pp. 13-14, Manipulation Checks; p. 14, Statistical Approach

confirmed.statement: The design is randomized, but the analyzed groups are not the randomized groups. AI-arm trials without chat data were dropped (24 percent of low-agency and 38 percent of high-agency trials), 22 AI-arm participants were 'completely excluded from the analysis', and the control arm had no matching exclusion. The authors write that this 'somewhat compromised the random assignment'. The form records the per-protocol analysis in participants.exclusions and eligibility.reason, so this is a caveat on the contrasts, not a coding error.
confirmed.locator: pp. 13-14, Manipulation Checks; p. 20, Limitations; p. 39, Treatment Noncompliance

confirmed.statement: Full-text search: assignment of submitters to conditions appears only on p. 2 ('experimentally assigned'), p. 11 ('randomly assigned'), p. 17 ('experimentally assigning'), and p. 20 ('random assignment'). The other 'random' hits are random selection of ideas for self-rating and evaluation, random effects in the mixed models, the 20 percent prompt-coding subsample, and model randomness.

summary: The paper states that individual submitters were randomly assigned to a high-agency or a low-agency arm with the same gpt-3.5 chatbot, or to a human-only control with no chatbot (p. 11; abstract, p. 2; Figure A1, p. 33), and every value in assignment, arms, and ai_tool matches the PDF, so criterion 1 holds. The only unsupported value is design_class online_rct, because the paper never says whether the community college students took the Qualtrics session remotely or under supervision, and the AI-arm-only exclusions that 'somewhat compromised the random assignment' (p. 20) are a caveat the form already records.
